Divide the noodles among bowls, add suông, shrimp, pork and pork hock, then ladle over hot broth and sprinkle with scallions. Serve with greens, fermented soybean sauce or tamarind fish sauce.
4 full bowls with shrimp-paste suông, pork, shrimp and fresh vegetables.
About 2 hours 45 minutes, including a 1-hour chill for the shrimp paste.
Pat the peeled shrimp dry before pounding and mixing so the paste turns springy instead of loose.
Chill the shrimp paste before shaping to help the suông hold its tapered form in the broth.
Simmer the broth gently and skim it often for a clean, naturally sweet flavor.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Clear, naturally sweet broth with tender pork rind, fragrant pork and dried shrimp, and colorful vegetables that retain a slight crispness.

Canh bóng thả is a delicate soup served in old-style Hanoi Tết feasts. Chicken stock is blended with the cooking liquids from dried shrimp and pork tenderloin; pork rind and vegetables are cooked just until tender so they keep their color and gentle bite.
Arrange the pork rind, vegetables, tenderloin and dried shrimp in bowls. Pour over piping-hot broth and finish with cilantro and pepper.
4 bowls of light soup with pork rind, pork tenderloin, dried shrimp and vegetables.
About 3 hours, including 60–90 minutes to soak the pork rind.
Soak the pork rind in concentrated glutinous-rice washing water until expanded, then deodorize it with ginger and rice wine and rinse well.
Skim the stock as it simmers and remove excess fat for a clear, delicate soup.
Heat the pork rind only until tender; long cooking can make it soft and limp.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Phu Tho Bánh Tai Rice Dumplings
fields: Soft, slightly chewy white rice dough folded into curved half moons around a moist, peppery pork and shallot filling.

Bánh tai is a savory everyday dumpling from Phú Thọ town: soft, chewy rice dough encloses pork shoulder seasoned with shallot, pepper and fish sauce, then is shaped into a curved ear-like half moon and steamed. Bếp Việt edited this family batch from the process introduced by the Phú Thọ Tourism Information and Promotion Center.
Serve hot as soon as the dumplings leave the steamer; pair with lightly seasoned fish sauce or pickled vegetables.
About 12 small steamed bánh tai dumplings, served hot.
About 4 hours 10 minutes, including a 3-hour rice soak.
Thi Xa Phu Tho banh tai
Soak the rice long enough for fine milling; add cold water gradually while kneading so the dough does not become too wet.
Pound and knead the dough while warm until smooth, pliable and free of cracks.
Shape a gentle curve and avoid overfilling so the seam stays closed while steaming.
A firm, chewy amber cake with fragrant rice and ginger notes and a sesame topping; once cool, it is firm enough to slice.

Banh to is a sweet sticky rice cake associated with Tet in Quang Nam. Sources describe glutinous rice, block cane sugar, ginger and sesame, steamed in a banana-leaf-lined mold. This is a small home batch using ready-ground glutinous rice flour and a shorter steaming time suited to a home mold; its proportions are not presented as a local bakery's formula.
Let the cake cool and firm before slicing. Eat it soft or pan-fry the slices in a little oil until the outside turns golden.
One round cake about 18 cm across, cut into 10–12 thin slices.
About 4 hours 25 minutes, including steaming and cooling until firm.
steamed cake with block cane sugar
Let the syrup cool slightly before mixing it into the flour to prevent lumps.
Line the mold bottom completely with banana leaf and leave a little headroom for the cake to expand.
Keep the steamer water at a steady simmer and top it up with hot water if needed during the long steam.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
A fragrant roll with pepper and banana-leaf aromas, a smooth rosy-brown interior and a savory, gently springy beef texture.

Da Nang's tourism portal describes chả bò as a local beef sausage made with trimmed beef thigh, finely ground and seasoned with onion, garlic, pepper, chili, sugar and fish sauce, then wrapped in banana leaves and boiled. Bếp Việt has adapted a small home batch, keeping the beef cold while grinding and forming two short rolls so they cook evenly.
Let the sausage cool slightly before slicing. Serve with pickled vegetables, herbs, baguette or beef porridge.
Two small sausage rolls, about 600 g total, sliced and served with pickles or baguette.
About 1 hour 35 minutes, including a short cooling rest after boiling.
Chill the beef, grinder bowl and water before grinding so the meat stays cold and cohesive.
Wrap two short rolls tightly and seal the leaves so water cannot seep inside.
Use a clean food thermometer to confirm the center of the sausage reaches 71°C before removing it from the pot.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Ca Mau Ốc Len with Coconut
fields: The cooked snails are springy and fragrant with lemongrass and garlic, coated in a lightly sweet and savory coconut sauce finished with Vietnamese coriander.

Ốc len snails live in mangrove forests and coastal mudflats in Ca Mau. Local reporting describes soaking them to release grit, cutting the pointed tail, then cooking them with coconut milk, garlic, lemongrass and Vietnamese coriander. Bếp Việt has edited a home batch using snails from a reliable food supplier and cooking them thoroughly.
Serve hot in a shallow bowl with the coconut sauce. Bread can be used to mop up the sauce.
One hot plate of snails for four people to share as a snack or starter.
About 1 hour 30 minutes, mostly for soaking the snails to release grit.
Ca Mau oc len with coconut
Choose live snails with intact shells; discard dead snails or any with an off smell before soaking.
Cut just enough of the pointed tail to open the shell for suction; do not cut so deeply that the snail breaks apart.
Cook at a steady simmer until the snails are fully cooked; discard shells that remain closed or smell unusual.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Beef Offal in Coconut and Five-Spice Broth
fields: Tender but slightly springy offal absorbs five-spice and coconut; the amber broth smells of ginger, star anise and cinnamon.
Beef Offal in Coconut and Five-Spice Broth

Beef pha lau is a familiar street food in Ho Chi Minh City. Sources describe beef offal cleaned carefully, seasoned with five-spice and aromatics, then simmered in coconut water. Bếp Việt has adapted a home-size batch with commonly available beef tripe, cooked until tender and served with baguette, Vietnamese coriander and a sweet-sour dipping sauce.
Cut the offal into bite-size pieces and ladle over hot broth. Serve with crisp baguette, Vietnamese coriander and a lime dipping sauce.
Four small bowls of pha lau, served with baguette and Vietnamese coriander.
About 2 hours 40 minutes, including a 30-minute marinade before braising.
Rub the offal with ginger, vinegar and rice wine, then rinse thoroughly before blanching.
Brief blanching and rinsing reduce strong aromas without over-tightening the offal before braising.
Simmer gently until the thickest pieces are tender; taste after the coconut broth reduces because its saltiness becomes more concentrated.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Soft millet grains blend with mashed mung beans into a thick golden porridge with gentle sweetness; crisp sesame crackers add contrast.

Hoi An heritage records include millet sweet porridge among the offerings for the Doan Ngo festival. A recipe presented with guidance from a culinary artisan combines millet and mung beans and serves the porridge with toasted rice crackers for scooping. Bếp Việt has edited a plant-based batch without dairy or animal fat, cooked until thick enough to eat by spoon or with rice crackers.
Spoon the warm or cooled porridge into small bowls. Break toasted sesame rice crackers into pieces to scoop it up.
Four thick bowls of sweet porridge with toasted sesame rice crackers.
About 2 hours 5 minutes, including 1 hour for soaking the millet and mung beans.
Soak millet and mung beans separately so both soften evenly.
Stir gently but regularly once the millet thickens so it does not stick to the pot.
Add the sugar after the mung beans soften so you can adjust sweetness and thickness easily.

names: Mekong Delta Sesbania Flower Bánh Xèo
fields: Thin golden crepes with crisp edges, just-cooked shrimp and pork, bean sprouts and intact sesbania flowers; fresh greens and tamarind sauce balance the gentle richness.

Sesbania flower bánh xèo is associated with the Mekong Delta flood season, when the yellow blossoms are placed in the filling rather than served only as a side green. Bếp Việt edits a home batch with shrimp, pork belly, bean sprouts and seasonal sesbania flowers; a light coconut mixture makes the crepe fragrant while keeping it crisp. Use only flowers sold as food from a safe source, wash them well and drain thoroughly.
Serve hot. Break off a piece, wrap it with lettuce and herbs, then dip it in tamarind fish sauce. Do not stack the crepes for long, as trapped steam softens the crust.
About eight medium crepes, two per person, served with fresh greens and tamarind fish sauce.
About 1 hour 20 minutes, including 20 minutes for the batter to rest; frying time varies with pan size.
Rest the batter for 20 minutes, then stir again; if it is thick, add water a little at a time so it spreads thinly.
Dry the sesbania flowers after washing to reduce oil splatter and keep the crepes crisp.
Cover briefly to cook the filling, then uncover and keep the heat moderate until the edges dry and crisp.
Evenly cooked sticky rice in bamboo tubes, glossy and tender with a light roasted-bamboo aroma; serve with nutty sesame salt.

Cơm lam is a way of cooking glutinous rice in bamboo or reed tubes over a fire and is recorded across several Northwest provinces. Bếp Việt edits a home batch with overnight-soaked upland sticky rice, a little salt and ginger; the rice cooks tender and fragrant inside the young bamboo membrane. Families and local areas differ in seasoning, tube choice and accompaniments.

Let the tubes cool slightly, peel away the outer bamboo and keep the thin inner membrane attached to the rice. Cut into serving pieces and eat with sesame salt; grilled stream fish or pork can be served alongside.
Four small bamboo tubes, one per person; serve with sesame salt or grilled dishes.
About 9 hours 10 minutes, including overnight rice soaking; grilling time varies with tube size and coal heat.
what to serve with cơm lam
Soak and drain the rice well so it cooks evenly without a hard center.
Fill the tubes only about two-thirds full and leave room for the rice to expand.
Turn the tubes regularly over glowing coals; one side can char before the rice cooks if left facing the heat.
A hot bowl of thick, pleasantly chewy noodles with sweet crab meat and a clean, seafood-forward broth topped with a little scallion and cilantro.

Bánh canh ghẹ is a familiar seafood noodle soup in Vũng Tàu; its broth is commonly simmered with crab and pork bones for a rounded natural sweetness. Bếp Việt edits a home version with thick bánh canh noodles, blue swimmer crab, shallot and a little annatto oil for a warm, clear broth.
Place the noodles in bowls and ladle over boiling broth. Add the crab meat, claws, scallion and cilantro. Serve hot with pepper, lime and chili to taste.
Four medium bowls, each with one portion of crab and thick noodles.
About 1 hour 15 minutes for prep, broth and crab; fresh noodles shorten the cooking time.
Choose fresh crabs with intact shells; steaming them separately keeps the meat from breaking down in the broth.
Skim the pork-bone broth as it simmers for a clearer, cleaner flavor.
Blanch the noodles separately if they have excess surface starch, so the soup does not become too thick.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Krông Pa One-Sun Beef with Ant-Egg Salt
One-sun beef with muối kiến vàng
fields: Warm one-sun beef with lightly charred edges and tender slices inside; muối kiến vàng adds savory, tangy, spicy and aromatic notes.
One-sun beef with muối kiến vàng

One-sun beef served with muối kiến vàng is a regional pairing associated with Krông Pa, Gia Lai and Central Highlands food culture. The beef is seasoned and dried in the sun for a day before it is cooked for serving; this Bếp Việt home version uses commercially prepared, labeled one-sun beef, quickly grilled and served with food-grade ant-egg salt.
Rest the beef for 3 minutes, then slice across the grain. Serve with muối kiến vàng, herbs or rice paper, following the package's storage and cooking instructions.
One 500 g plate of prepared beef to share with vegetables and rice paper for 3–4 people.
About 22 minutes using prepared one-sun beef; the traditional seasoning and sun-drying time is not part of this reheating recipe.
Choose labeled one-sun beef with a clear use-by date and storage directions; thaw in the refrigerator if frozen.
Preheat the grill and cook briefly on each side; prolonged grilling makes the meat dry and tough.
Muối kiến vàng may contain insect allergens; check ingredients and avoid it if you have a related allergy.

names: Quảng Bình Cháo Canh with Snakehead Fish
fields: Thick, tender noodles in a hot broth with lightly turmeric-colored snakehead fish and just-cooked mustard greens; the broth is gently thickened, not like rice porridge.

Cháo canh is a rustic specialty of Quảng Bình. Despite the word cháo, the dish is a noodle soup made with thick wheat- or rice-flour noodles, snakehead fish, meat and mustard greens. Bếp Việt edits a fish version with pork-bone stock, củ nén and turmeric; fresh noodles are used to simplify the home preparation.
Serve while piping hot with scallion and black pepper. Crispy ram rolls can accompany the bowl as they do in local servings; add chili if desired.
Four medium bowls, each with thick dough noodles, snakehead fish and mustard greens.
About 1 hour 5 minutes with fresh noodles; cooking time varies with the noodle type.
Choose fresh or packaged cháo canh noodles and follow the package cooking time so they do not break down.
Cook the fish just until done, remove all bones carefully and strain the poaching liquid for a clean broth.
Add the mustard greens at the end; once the broth returns to a boil, turn off the heat to keep the greens bright and crisp.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Each warm cake has a neat slender shape, a tender ivory rice casing and a savory pork filling with lightly crisp mushrooms and fragrant shallots.

Phu Nhi rice cakes are a Xu Doai specialty made from wet-ground rice batter and filled with pork, wood-ear mushrooms and shallots before being wrapped in leaves and boiled. Bếp Việt adapts the traditional technique for a small home batch, stirring the batter until smooth and pliable without letting it become pasty.
Unwrap while warm and enjoy with pickled vegetables or a little dipping sauce. Re-steam briefly if the cakes cool; avoid boiling them again, which can make the casing waterlogged.
About eight slender cakes, two per person, served warm with a light dipping sauce.
About 4 hours 35 minutes, including three hours to soak the rice; the rice can be soaked overnight.
Vietnamese pork rice cakes in leaves
Soak the rice until soft, then blend it thoroughly; strain if any coarse grains remain.
Stir the batter over low heat until just thickened and still pliable. Overcooked batter is difficult to spread around the filling.
Wrap the leaves snugly but leave room for expansion, then tie gently so the cakes cook evenly without splitting.

names: Shrimp and pork bánh ram ít
fields: A golden crisp base supports a tender ivory dumpling with savory shrimp and pork, a little scallion oil and a gentle chili-lime dip.
Shrimp and pork bánh ram ít

Hue bánh ram ít combines two textures in one bite: a soft glutinous-rice dumpling filled with shrimp and pork, set on a crisp fried rice base. Bếp Việt edits a home-sized batch with lightly seasoned filling and a sweet-sour fish sauce for serving.
Assemble each dumpling on its crispy base just before serving. Eat warm with lightly sweetened garlic-chili fish sauce to balance the richness and chewiness.
About twelve small dumplings, three per person, served while the crispy bases are fresh.
About 1 hour 35 minutes, including a 15-minute dough rest; fry the bases in small batches to keep them crisp.
Add warm water to the glutinous-rice flour gradually until the dough is smooth and not sticky.
Steam the bases first, let them cool and pat dry before frying to make them crisp with less splatter.
Cook the filling until fairly dry and let it cool before wrapping so the dough does not become soggy.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
A pale-golden coconut broth carries the natural sweetness of pumpkin and root vegetables. Each piece of vegetable, mushroom and tofu skin stays distinct, creating a gently rich plant-based soup.

Canh kiểm is a Southern Vietnamese vegetarian soup that simmers a variety of vegetables in coconut liquid and is often served at vegetarian meals and offerings. Bếp Việt edits a home version with pumpkin, sweet potato, taro, green banana, long beans, mushrooms, tofu skin and peanuts; the ingredients are added in stages so tender vegetables keep their shape.
Serve hot with rice or vermicelli. Ladle gently so the vegetables stay intact; if using thick coconut cream, dilute it to keep the broth from becoming heavy.
One pot of about 1.5 litres, served with steamed rice or fresh rice vermicelli.
Vietnamese vegetarian pumpkin and taro soup
Briefly pan-sear the taro to help it hold its shape and develop a nutty flavor.
Add pumpkin and long beans after the slower-cooking roots so they do not overcook.
Use coconut milk in moderation and season at the end, since the vegetables vary in natural sweetness.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Mushroom and tofu bún in Hue style
fields: A hot bowl with clear lemongrass-scented broth, gentle mushroom sweetness, golden tofu, tender chewy wheat gluten and green vegetables makes a light but satisfying meal.
Mushroom and tofu bún in Hue style

Hue vegetarian bún is a fragrant noodle soup built around mushrooms and lemongrass, served with rice vermicelli, fried tofu, wheat gluten, bamboo shoots and greens. Bếp Việt edits a fully plant-based home version with a vegetable-and-mushroom broth; check packaged seasonings to avoid animal-derived ingredients.

Blanch the noodles separately, place them in bowls, then ladle over the simmering broth with mushrooms, bamboo shoots, tofu and wheat gluten. Add herbs, pepper or chili and serve at once so the noodles stay springy.
Four generous bowls with mushrooms, tofu, bamboo shoots and wheat gluten.
About 1 hour 20 minutes, including 20 minutes to soak bamboo shoots and mushrooms; pre-cooked fresh bamboo shoots shorten the preparation.
Boil dried bamboo shoots twice, changing the water, and taste them before cooking to reduce bitterness and strong aromas.
Sauté the mushrooms and wheat gluten before adding them to deepen the flavor of both the toppings and broth.
Use leek in place of onion and garlic if desired, and verify that packaged seasoning is fully plant-based.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Each small square cake has a glossy dark casing with the fragrance of ramie leaves, a sweet mung-bean and coconut center, a hint of molasses and a lightly nutty sesame finish.

Tu Tru bánh gai from Mia village in Tho Xuan is known for a dark glutinous-rice casing made with ramie leaves, a mung-bean and coconut filling, gentle molasses sweetness and sesame. Bếp Việt adapts a small batch with softened dried ramie leaves and ordinary home equipment; the parcels are wrapped in banana leaf, steamed and cooled so the casing becomes pleasantly chewy.
Let the cakes cool completely before peeling the inner leaf, since the casing is sticky. Serve in small pieces with hot tea; briefly steam again if a refrigerated cake becomes firm.
About eight small cakes, two per person, served cooled with hot tea.
About 4 hours 25 minutes, including three hours to soak the mung beans and ramie leaves; these can be soaked ahead.
Vietnamese mung bean coconut ramie cake
Cook the ramie leaves until very soft, then blend or pound finely; fibrous leaves make the casing rough.
Cook the filling until it just holds together when rolled; drying it too much makes the center crumbly.
Wrap the parcels securely and steam over steady medium heat. Let them dry and cool before stacking so condensation does not collect on the leaves.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Bac Lieu spicy beef rice noodles
fields: A hot bowl of naturally golden-orange broth, tender but distinct beef slices, white vermicelli and fragrant Thai basil; add satay and chili separately to control the heat.

Bac Lieu spicy beef bún is known for its deep golden broth, the fragrant heat of satay and tender beef served with white rice vermicelli. Bếp Việt adapts a home batch with a lighter broth, keeping Thai basil, lime and chili salt as characteristic accompaniments.
Briefly blanch the noodles, arrange the beef and ladle over simmering broth. Serve with Thai basil, lime and chili salt; let each person add satay at the table.
Four medium bowls with spicy broth, beef and Thai basil; adjust the satay to taste.
About 2 hours 15 minutes, mostly for simmering the bones and tenderizing the beef.
Blanch the bones and beef briefly, then rinse them to reduce scum and odor in the broth.
Fry the satay gently and use enough for aroma and color without letting the chili burn.
Remove the beef as soon as tender, cool slightly and slice across the grain; keep the broth at a gentle simmer.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Black bánh chưng from Xu Lang
fields: A square cake with glossy dark glutinous rice, a nutty yellow mung-bean layer and tender pork; the color comes from the rice treatment, not charring.
Black bánh chưng from Xu Lang

Lang Son black bánh chưng is a Tay variation: glutinous rice is soaked in carefully filtered plant-ash water, then wrapped with mung beans and pork in dong leaves. Bếp Việt adapts a family batch; use only ash water confirmed safe for food and never burn unknown plants to make it.
Let the cake rest after boiling, press it lightly to drain, then slice with a clean knife. Serve with pickled onions or vegetables; refrigerate leftovers promptly and reheat thoroughly.
One family-sized square cake cut into eight pieces; serve warm or pan-fry after refrigeration.
About 20 hours, including eight hours of soaking and 10–12 hours of boiling; the rice can soak overnight.
black glutinous rice cake with mung bean and pork
soaking rice in food-grade ash water
Use only plant-ash water labeled or confirmed for food use; do not use ash from unidentified plants, contaminated materials or chemical-treated wood.
Soak the rice and mung beans separately and distribute the filling evenly so the center cooks through.
Keep the cake submerged during boiling, top up with boiling water and maintain a gentle boil; never let the pot run dry.
Thin golden cakes with pink shrimp visible on top and fragrant sweet potato; fresh greens and pickles balance the richness of the fried batter.

Hồ Tây shrimp cakes are associated with Hanoi's West Lake area: fresh shrimp and sweet-potato strands are coated in a light batter and fried until golden. Bếp Việt adapts a home batch with just enough batter to hold the cake together, serving the shrimp whole with greens, pickles and sweet-sour fish sauce.
Drain the cakes on a rack or absorbent paper and serve hot. Wrap with lettuce and herbs, add pickles and dip in sweet-sour fish sauce; do not cover the hot cakes, or steam will soften them.
About eight small cakes, two per person, served hot with fresh greens and sweet-sour dipping sauce.
About 1 hour 5 minutes, including ten minutes to rest the batter and make quick pickles.
Cut the sweet potato into short strands and pat dry so the batter holds and fries evenly.
Use only enough batter to coat the ingredients; keep the cakes thin rather than forming a thick pancake.
Keep the oil at a steady medium heat and fry in small batches; drain the cakes as soon as they come out.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Trảng Bàng bánh canh Tây Ninh
fields: A bowl of light broth with soft, springy rice noodles, tender pork and pork hock; fresh greens balance the broth's gentle savory richness.
Trảng Bàng bánh canh Tây Ninh

Trảng Bàng bánh canh is a Tay Ninh noodle soup made with thick rice-flour noodles, a clear pork broth, boiled pork and wild greens on the side. Bếp Việt adapts a home version with ready-made fresh noodles; choose seasonal greens such as herbs, perilla, fish mint and mildly sour leaves.
Blanch the noodles separately, ladle over hot broth and top with sliced pork and hock. Serve with seasonal wild greens, lime, chili and a small dish of pepper fish sauce for the pork.
Four bowls with rice-flour noodles, boiled pork and seasonal greens; divide the pork hock to taste.
About 2 hours 20 minutes, mostly to simmer the bones and cook the pork.
Blanch the bones and pork first, rinse well, then simmer to keep the broth clear and mild.
Lift the pork out as soon as it is tender; leaving it in the pot too long can make the slices dry and crumbly.
Cook the noodles according to their package directions; rinse briefly if heavily dusted with starch before adding broth.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Golden, thick porridge with softened but distinct rice grains, turmeric-scented eel on top, and rau răm, rice-paddy herb and pepper for a warming finish.

Vinh eel porridge is a specialty of Nghe An, pairing slowly cooked rice porridge with field eel sautéed in turmeric, local shallots and chili. Bếp Việt adapts a home method that keeps the eel pieces intact, uses carefully strained eel-bone stock and lets each diner adjust the heat.
Ladle hot porridge into bowls and top with the sautéed eel. Scatter rau răm, rice-paddy herb, scallions and pepper. Serve with bánh mướt or bread and add extra chili if desired.
Four bowls of thick porridge topped with separately sautéed eel, herbs and chili to taste; serve with bánh mướt or bread if desired.
About 1 hour 50 minutes, including eel preparation, stock and porridge simmering.
Strain the eel-bone stock through a fine sieve so no small bones remain in the porridge.
Simmer the rice gently and avoid vigorous stirring so the grains open without breaking into paste.
Sauté the eel separately with turmeric and local shallots, stirring only as needed so the pieces stay whole and moist.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Nha Trang rice cakes with shrimp and quail eggs
Nha Trang bánh căn with shrimp and quail eggs
fields: Small cakes with lightly golden edges and soft centers, topped with shrimp or quail egg and served hot with scallion oil, fresh herbs, green mango and fish sauce.
Nha Trang bánh căn with shrimp and quail eggs

Nha Trang bánh căn are small rice-flour cakes cooked individually in clay molds, with shrimp or quail eggs on top. Bếp Việt adapts a family batch using a multi-well pan and scallion-fish sauce, served with herbs and green mango to balance the savory topping.
Serve the cakes as soon as they leave the mold. Add a little scallion oil, herbs and green mango, then dip lightly in fish sauce or scallion fish sauce.
About 24 small cakes, six per person, served with greens, green mango and dipping sauce.
About 1 hour 25 minutes, including resting the batter and cooking the cakes in batches.
bánh căn with shrimp and quail egg
Resting the batter for about 30 minutes helps the rice flour hydrate; stir again before each batch because the flour settles.
Preheat the mold and brush it with only a thin film of oil. Cover briefly so the top cooks while the edges set crisp.
Do not overfill each well. Cook shrimp and quail egg through before serving.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Da Nang steamed scad with rice-paper rolls
Da Nang scad rolls with water spinach
Central Vietnamese steamed scad rice-paper rolls
ingredients: Fresh greens and young water spinach
fields: Tender steamed scad scented with lemongrass and scallions, wrapped in rice paper with fresh herbs, young water spinach and vermicelli; served with fish sauce or fermented anchovy dipping sauce.
Da Nang scad rolls with water spinach
Central Vietnamese steamed scad rice-paper rolls

Steamed scad wrapped in rice paper is a simple coastal Da Nang meal. The fish is steamed with lemongrass, scallion and chili to keep its natural sweetness, then rolled with herbs, noodles and vegetables. Bếp Việt adapts a family-sized portion and includes a safe doneness check.
Flake the fish into pieces and check carefully for pin bones. Wrap with rice paper, noodles and greens; dip in the sweet-sour fish sauce or prepared fermented anchovy sauce.
Four servings of steamed fish with rice paper, fresh vermicelli, greens and dipping sauce.
About 45 minutes; steaming is quick, while most preparation time goes to the greens and dipping sauce.
Choose fresh fish with clear eyes and firm flesh; keep the raw-fish knife and board separate from the greens.
Steam just until done so the flesh stays moist. For thicker fish, extend the cooking time and check that the flesh next to the bone is opaque.
Strain the steaming liquid and bring it to a boil before using it to thin the dipping sauce.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Fresh greens and young water spinach
A hot bowl of thick, tender-chewy noodles with just-cooked shrimp and fish, scallions and pepper in a clear, savory seafood broth.

Quang Binh chao canh is not smooth rice porridge: it is a hearty soup with thick, pleasantly chewy handmade noodles and a flavorful seafood broth. Bếp Việt adapts a home pot with shrimp and fish, keeping the noodles as the defining feature and seasoning lightly to let the seafood broth shine.
Divide the noodles and seafood among bowls and ladle over the hot broth. Finish with scallions, coriander and pepper; serve chili separately.
Four hot bowls of thick noodles with shrimp, fish and broth.
About 1 hour 35 minutes including dough resting; fresh store-bought noodles shorten the preparation.
If rolling the noodles at home, dust them lightly so they do not stick; shake off excess dry flour before adding them to the pot.
Cook the noodles in a gentle boil and stir the bottom of the pot at the start so they stay separate.
Add the fish near the end and maintain a moderate simmer so it cooks through without breaking apart.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Quy Nhon sizzling pancakes with fresh shrimp
fields: Small golden turmeric pancakes with crisp edges, earth shrimp and bean sprouts, wrapped in fresh greens and dipped in sweet-sour fish sauce.

Quy Nhon bánh xèo tôm nhảy are usually small, crisp-edged pancakes filled with fresh local earth shrimp and eaten with greens. Bếp Việt keeps the cakes small, the batter thin and the shrimp visible, distinguishing this style from larger, richer coconut-milk versions found elsewhere.
Serve the pancakes hot with lettuce, herbs and fish sauce. Break off a bite-sized piece, wrap it in greens and dip lightly to keep the edge crisp.
About 12 small pancakes, three per person, served with greens and sweet-sour fish sauce.
About 55 minutes including resting the batter and cooking the pancakes in batches.
Quy Nhon bánh xèo tôm nhảy
Spread only a thin layer of batter in a small pan; cover briefly so the shrimp cooks, then uncover to release steam and crisp the shell.
Pat the shrimp dry before adding it to the pan to prevent splatter and soggy batter.
Cook over medium heat and wait for the edges to turn golden and release before folding or removing the pancake.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Hue Cồn Hến mixed clam vermicelli
ingredients: Pork crackling or crispy pork skin
fields: A bowl of vermicelli topped with fragrant clams, herbs and banana blossom, finished with peanuts, sesame and pork crackling; served with hot clam broth and chili shrimp paste on the side.

Hue bún hến is a mixed bowl of rice vermicelli with sautéed clams, fresh herbs, peanuts, rice crackers and fermented shrimp paste; hot clam broth is commonly served on the side. Bếp Việt adapts a family version with fresh clams, keeping the savory, spicy flavor while serving shrimp paste and chili separately for individual seasoning.
Divide vermicelli among bowls and top with sautéed clams and greens. Sprinkle with peanuts, sesame and crackling. Serve with hot clam broth; add shrimp paste or chili to taste and mix before eating.
Four bowls of mixed vermicelli with clams; hot clam broth is served separately for pouring as desired.
About 1 hour 20 minutes, including 30 minutes to soak the clams and release grit.
Soak clams in clean water with a little salt to release sand, changing the water several times; discard cracked or foul-smelling shells.
Boil until shells open and discard any that remain closed; strain the cooking liquid finely to remove grit.
Wash and drain the greens and banana blossom thoroughly; mix them in just before serving to keep their crunch.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Pork crackling or crispy pork skin

names: Boiled Tiên Yên hill chicken with lime leaf
fields: The chicken is just cooked, with moist, firm white meat and glossy golden skin; cut into serving pieces and finish with finely sliced lime leaf and lime-pepper salt.
Boiled Tiên Yên hill chicken with lime leaf

Tiên Yên chicken is known for fragrant, sweet meat, a firm bite and naturally golden skin. Bếp Việt keeps the preparation simple so the chicken remains the focus, adding a little ginger, shallot and lime leaf. Serve warm with lime-pepper salt or ginger dipping sauce.
Let the chicken rest briefly, cut through the joints and arrange on a platter with lime leaf. Serve warm with salt, pepper and lime; the cooking broth can be seasoned and served as soup.
One chicken weighing about 1.4 kg, cut into 8–10 pieces and shared by four people.
About 1 hour 15 minutes, including 45 minutes of simmering and a 10-minute rest; timing depends on the chicken's size.
Choose traceable Tiên Yên chicken. If it is unavailable, use a similarly sized free-range chicken to keep a firm texture.
Keep the pot at a gentle simmer rather than a rolling boil so the skin is less likely to split and the meat cooks evenly. Timing depends on the bird's size and age.
Use a food thermometer to check that the thickest part of the thigh reaches at least 74°C. Rest the chicken in the hot broth for about 10 minutes before cutting.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Purple bánh tét from Cần Thơ
Magenta-leaf bánh tét with pork and salted egg
fields: Each slice has a chewy violet rice layer around yellow mung beans, tender pork and salted egg yolk; the cross-section is round and holds together without becoming mushy.
Purple bánh tét from Cần Thơ
Magenta-leaf bánh tét with pork and salted egg

Bình Thủy bánh tét lá cẩm has naturally purple sticky rice wrapped around mung beans, pork and salted duck egg yolk. Bếp Việt adapts a one-roll family batch, coloring the rice with magenta-leaf infusion, mixing it with coconut milk, then wrapping it in banana leaves and simmering until fully cooked.
Let the roll cool slightly, then use a sharp knife to cut slices about 1.5 cm thick. Serve as a light meal or pan-sear both sides for a fragrant, lightly crisp surface.
One medium roll, cut into about 16 slices; serve two slices per person as a main or side.
About 9 hours 30 minutes, including 4 hours of rice soaking and 4 hours 30 minutes of boiling; soak the rice overnight if convenient.
bánh tét with pork and salted egg
Soak the rice in strained magenta-leaf water for an even color; drain it thoroughly before mixing in coconut milk.
Wrap firmly but leave room for the rice to expand. Seal the banana-leaf ends so cooking water does not enter the filling.
Keep the roll submerged throughout boiling and top up with hot water. Cool leftovers promptly and refrigerate.

names: Trảng Bàng dew-wetted rice paper rolls with boiled pork
Trảng Bàng rice paper rolls with pork
fields: Pliable rice paper wraps boiled pork, vermicelli and greens without tearing; serve with pineapple fermented-fish sauce balanced between salty, sweet and sour.
Trảng Bàng rice paper rolls with pork

Trảng Bàng's signature rolls pair soft, pliable dew-wetted rice paper with boiled pork, fresh rice vermicelli and a generous selection of greens, especially local forest herbs. Bếp Việt adapts an easy home platter with familiar herbs and pineapple fermented-fish sauce for a savory, fresh balance.
Arrange the rice paper, pork, vermicelli, herbs and vegetables separately so everyone can roll their own. Dew-wetted rice paper is usually ready to use without dipping in water.
About 16 medium rolls, served as a shared main meal for four.
About 55 minutes to prepare the greens, boil the pork and make the dipping sauce; assemble the rolls at the table.
Tây Ninh rice paper and forest herbs
Do not soak pliable dew-wetted rice paper. Keep unused sheets covered so they do not dry out.
Start the pork in cold water for even cooking. Check the thickest piece with a food thermometer; it should reach at least 71°C before slicing.
Wash the greens thoroughly under clean running water and drain well. Add fermented-fish sauce gradually because saltiness varies by brand.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Cẩm Kim Hội An bánh bèo rice cakes
Quảng Nam bánh bèo with shrimp and pork
fields: Small bowls of opaque white rice cake with a soft, moderately thick texture, topped with orange-brown minced shrimp and pork, fried shallots and scallion oil; serve with fish sauce on the side or spooned over.
Quảng Nam bánh bèo with shrimp and pork

Cẩm Kim bánh bèo is a rustic Hội An breakfast, prepared in the Quảng Nam style with thicker, soft rice cakes and a minced shrimp-and-pork topping. Bếp Việt adapts a family batch steamed in small bowls, finished with scallion oil and fried shallots and served with mildly spicy fish sauce.
Serve the cakes as soon as they come out of the steamer, topped with hot shrimp-and-pork mixture, scallion oil and fried shallots. Add a little fish sauce to each bowl or serve it on the side.
About 16 small bowls, four per person; serve hot with seasoned fish sauce.
About 1 hour 10 minutes, including 20 minutes for the batter to rest and steaming in batches.
bánh bèo with minced shrimp and pork
Stir the batter again before pouring because rice flour settles. A moderate layer lets the cakes steam evenly in small bowls.
Preheat the empty bowls in the steamer so the batter sets smoothly; avoid opening the lid repeatedly while the cakes cook.
Season the Quảng Nam-style shrimp-and-pork topping lightly so the shrimp's sweetness remains clear; adjust the fish sauce at the table.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Central Highlands cassava-leaf soup with bitter eggplant and dried fish
Cassava-leaf and bitter-eggplant soup with dried fish
ingredients: Young cassava leaves prepared as food
fields: Soft cassava leaves simmer in a green-brown broth with intact pieces of bitter eggplant and lightly smoky dried fish; the flavor is gently bitter, nutty and moderately salty.
Cassava-leaf and bitter-eggplant soup with dried fish

Cassava-leaf soup is an everyday forest-vegetable dish in many Central Highlands communities. Young cassava leaves are pounded and simmered with bitter eggplant and dried fish, creating a nutty, gently bitter flavor associated with the highlands. Bếp Việt adapts a home version and emphasizes careful processing of the leaves before they enter the pot.
Ladle the soup hot into bowls and serve with steamed rice. Taste for salt only after the dried fish has released its flavor; serve fresh chili separately if desired.
About 1.4 liters of soup, divided among four bowls and served with steamed rice.
About 1 hour 5 minutes, including careful leaf preparation, a separate brief boil and a second simmer until fully tender.
Use only young cassava leaves sold for food and process them safely; raw cassava leaves contain cyanogenic compounds.

Pound the leaves thoroughly for at least 10 minutes, wash them with plenty of clean water, boil separately for 8–10 minutes and discard all the cooking water. Then simmer them in the soup until very tender.
Dried fish is already salty, so rinse it briefly, toast it and add fish sauce only at the end. Reduce the bitter eggplant if diners are new to its flavor.
Young cassava leaves prepared as food
Soft white rice dumplings sit in amber sugarcane-molasses syrup with warming ginger and a light sprinkle of toasted sesame; the syrup remains clear rather than cloudy.

Coóng phù is a round glutinous-rice dumpling associated with the Tày community in Cao Bằng and is often enjoyed hot in cold weather. Bếp Việt adapts a home version using glutinous-rice flour, ginger and sugarcane molasses; the dumplings are boiled separately before being served in the syrup so it stays clear and fragrant.
Divide the dumplings and hot ginger-molasses syrup among small bowls. Add toasted sesame or crushed peanuts if desired and serve while warm.
Four small bowls of hot coóng phù, served as an afternoon treat or winter dessert.
About 40 minutes to knead the dough, boil the dumplings and prepare the ginger-molasses syrup.
Add warm water gradually until the dough is smooth, pliable and no longer sticky.
Boil the dumplings separately, remove them when they float, then add them to the ginger syrup to keep the syrup clear.
Molasses sweetness varies; dilute and taste it before adding extra sugar.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Ivory rice dumplings, some showing their golden mung-bean filling, sit in hot ginger syrup with a restrained coconut-milk drizzle, roasted peanuts and coconut.

Thắng dền is a small glutinous-rice dumpling from Hà Giang, commonly filled with mung bean and served in hot ginger-sugar syrup. Bếp Việt prepares a home-style version with a light coconut-milk drizzle, roasted peanuts and shredded coconut; adjust the sweetness to taste.
Divide the dumplings and ginger syrup among bowls. Drizzle with warm coconut milk, add crushed peanuts and shredded coconut, and serve while hot.
Four small bowls, each with 5–6 mung-bean-filled rice dumplings in ginger syrup.
About 1 hour, including steaming the filling, shaping the dumplings and cooking the ginger syrup.
Cool the mung-bean filling completely before wrapping; keep each filling ball smaller than its dough wrapper.
Knead until pliable but not wet; if the dough cracks, moisten your hands instead of pouring in a lot of water.
Keep the ginger syrup at a gentle simmer and add the coconut milk only when serving so the ginger remains distinct.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Chewy golden turmeric noodles are topped with glossy lemongrass-and-turmeric braised frog and a little concentrated broth; peanuts, fresh herbs and crisp sesame rice crackers add texture.

Mì Quảng ếch is a familiar variation of Đà Nẵng mì Quảng. Frog is marinated and braised with lemongrass, củ nén and turmeric to make a fragrant, concentrated topping. Bếp Việt adapts a home version with just enough broth to moisten the wide noodles, served with fresh herbs, roasted peanuts and sesame rice crackers.
Place the noodles in bowls, top with frog and a little concentrated broth rather than filling the bowl. Serve with fresh herbs, lime, chili, roasted peanuts and sesame rice crackers.
Four bowls with about 150 g fresh noodles and 2–3 pieces of braised frog per serving, with herbs and rice crackers.
About 1 hour 10 minutes, including marinating, braising and preparing the fresh herbs.
Choose cleaned frog legs from a reputable supplier, pat dry before marinating, and cook fully; keep raw marinade away from ready-to-eat herbs.
Củ nén, also called hành tăm, gives a distinctive aroma; shallots can replace it if needed, though the flavor will differ.
Keep the topping broth concentrated and use only a small amount in each bowl.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Hậu Giang fish-cake and bitter-melon hotpot
Lẩu cá thát lát khổ qua
Bitter melon hotpot with fish cake
fields: A clear, savory broth holds ivory fish-cake balls and bright green bitter-melon slices; scallions and a little chili add aroma, while the bitterness remains gentle on the finish.
Lẩu cá thát lát khổ qua
Bitter melon hotpot with fish cake

Lẩu cá thát lát khổ qua pairs the springy, sweet fish of Hậu Giang with the clean bitterness of bitter melon. Bếp Việt adapts a home hotpot with pork-bone broth, daikon and mushrooms; the fish is kneaded into tender balls and added near serving time.
Keep the hotpot at a gentle simmer and add bitter melon and other vegetables in small batches to keep them fresh. Serve with rice vermicelli, fish sauce and chili, or steamed rice.
One small hotpot for four people, served with fresh rice vermicelli or steamed rice.
About 1 hour 25 minutes, including simmering the pork-bone broth and preparing the fish balls.
lẩu cá thát lát khổ qua
If using pre-ground fish, check the cold chain and ingredients; knead chilled fish in one direction until elastic so the balls hold together.
Season the broth lightly before adding the fish; ground fish may already be seasoned, so taste again after it cooks.
Add bitter melon shortly before serving and avoid overcooking to preserve its green color and gentle bitterness.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm
Small hand-wrapped cakes have a softly curved hunchback shape and deep-green dong leaves; the cut face shows naturally green sticky rice around a savory mung-bean and pork-belly filling.

Bánh chưng gù is a small hand-wrapped sticky-rice cake associated with the Tày people of Hà Giang. Bếp Việt adapts the Ngọc Đường style using rice naturally tinted green with leaf ginger, mung beans and pork belly wrapped in dong leaves and simmered until the rice is tender. It requires advance preparation and long cooking.
Let the cakes drain and cool slightly before cutting into halves or thick slices. Serve warm with pickled onions or pickled vegetables, or as a filling breakfast during Tết.
Four small hunchback-shaped cakes, one per person or halved for a festive meal.
About 16 hours in total, including 6 hours of soaking and 9 hours of boiling; soak the rice and beans ahead.
Soak the rice and mung beans separately; drain them well before wrapping so the cakes cook evenly without becoming wet.
Wrap each cake tightly by hand into a small curved shape, but do not compress the rice so firmly that it cannot expand; tie the leaves securely.
Keep the cakes submerged in water for 8–10 hours and top up with boiling water as needed; never let the pot run dry or expose the cakes.

names: Thai-Style Buffalo Skin and Water-Taro Soup (Son La)
fields: A lightly thickened bowl with soft, nutty water-taro stems, tender chewy buffalo skin, wild eggplant and herbs; warm mắc khén aroma complements the naturally savory broth.

Canh bon is a familiar soup in the meals of some Thai communities in Son La. Bếp Việt's edited home recipe keeps the documented ingredients: prepared bon stems, tender buffalo skin, wild eggplant, mắc khén and herbs. The long simmer is stated clearly so cooks can plan ahead.
Ladle the hot soup into deep bowls, dividing the bon stems and buffalo skin evenly. Serve with hot rice and offer fresh chili separately so each person can adjust the heat.
One bowl per person, served hot with rice and the other dishes in a family meal.
About 6 hours, including preparation, a five-hour buffalo-skin simmer and cooking the bon stems and vegetables until tender.
water-taro stems and buffalo skin soup

Buy bon stems intended for cooking from a trusted food seller. Wear gloves while peeling, rinse and soak in lightly salted water. Cook until completely tender; never taste uncooked or partly cooked bon.
Clean the buffalo skin and simmer it until tender before adding the bon. A pressure cooker can shorten this stage; follow the appliance instructions and check tenderness before continuing.
Add mắc khén and fresh herbs near the end to preserve their aroma. Season gradually because the buffalo skin and vegetables may vary in saltiness.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Hòa Bình Chicken Soup with Sour Bamboo Shoots and Hạt Dổi
Chicken and sour bamboo-shoot soup with hạt dổi
Hòa Bình chicken and sour bamboo shoots
fields: A clear pale-golden broth with mild sourness, tender chicken pieces that hold their shape, lightly crisp bamboo shoots and the warm aroma of toasted hạt dổi.
Chicken and sour bamboo-shoot soup with hạt dổi
Hòa Bình chicken and sour bamboo shoots

Chicken soup with sour bamboo shoots and hạt dổi is associated with meals in Hòa Bình, where fermented bamboo shoots and toasted forest nutmeg bring a warm, tangy aroma. Bếp Việt's home version keeps the local flavor profile and simmers chicken and bamboo shoots gently until tender.

Ladle equal portions of chicken, bamboo shoots and broth into bowls. Finish with scallions and cilantro and serve hot with steamed rice. Taste the broth before adding salt or fish sauce if the bamboo shoots are already salty.
One bowl containing chicken and bamboo shoots per person, served hot with rice.
About 1 hour 20 minutes, including preparation, a short marinade and gently simmering the chicken with bamboo shoots until tender.
chicken soup with sour bamboo shoots and hạt dổi
Hòa Bình sour bamboo chicken soup
Taste the bamboo shoots before cooking. Briefly boil and drain them if they are too salty or sharply sour. Discard bamboo shoots with an unusual smell, slime or abnormal surface film.
Toast hạt dổi briefly in a dry pan until fragrant, then grind it. Avoid scorching it, which can make the soup bitter.
Cook until the meat beside the bone is fully done. If using a food thermometer, the thickest part of the chicken should reach at least 74°C (165°F).
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Mộc Châu Mustard Greens Stir-Fried with Pork Belly
Moc Chau mustard greens stir-fried with pork belly
fields: Deep-green leaves with crisp stems, browned pork-belly slices and fragrant garlic; lightly savory with a gentle sweet finish from the greens.
Moc Chau mustard greens stir-fried with pork belly

C?i m?o is a familiar local green on the M?c Ch?u plateau; local references note that it can be stir-fried with smoked meat. B?p Vi?t edits this into a home-style version with fresh pork belly, cooked in a quick stir-fry so the stems stay just tender, the leaves remain green and the pan does not become watery.
Transfer the greens to a wide plate as soon as they are just cooked, sprinkle with ground pepper and serve hot with rice. Do not leave them in the pan, as residual heat will release water.
One small serving from a shared vegetable plate for four, alongside rice.
About 42 minutes, including washing, slicing, a short marinade and a quick high-heat stir-fry.
Separate thick stems from leaves and add the stems first so they cook through without over-wilting the leaves.
Stir-fry a small batch over high heat. An overcrowded pan steams the greens and makes them watery.
Soy sauce and oyster sauce are already salty, so taste before adding salt. Cooked smoked pork can replace fresh belly, but reduce the salty seasonings.

names: Northwest Vietnamese Grilled Chicken with Mắc Khén
Thai-style grilled chicken with mắc khén
fields: Golden-brown chicken with taut fragrant skin and juicy meat; mắc khén, ginger, lemongrass and a little chili create a warm aroma without overpowering the chicken.
Thai-style grilled chicken with mắc khén

Grilled chicken with mắc khén is a well-known dish of the Thai people in Vietnam's Northwest. Bếp Việt's home version portions the chicken into large pieces for easier grilling while keeping the regional flavor profile. The chicken is grilled over steady medium coals, allowed to render its own fat and brushed with the mắc khén seasoning near the end to keep the spice aromatic rather than burnt.
Cut the chicken into pieces, arrange on a platter and serve hot with rice, fresh greens or boiled vegetables. Offer chẳm chéo separately so diners can adjust the saltiness.
One quarter of the grilled chicken per person, served with rice or vegetables.
About 2 hours 15 minutes, including a one-hour marinade and grilling until fully cooked.
Grill over steady glowing coals rather than direct flames. Do not brush extra oil on the chicken; its own fat will render as it cooks.
Brush the mắc khén mixture on after the chicken surface has firmed. This helps release the aroma without scorching the spice.
Cook the chicken thoroughly. Use a thermometer to confirm the thickest section reaches at least 74°C (165°F). If using an oven, preheat it and rotate the tray midway for even cooking.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Moc Chau young beef with ginger and lemongrass
fields: Golden pieces of veal with lightly crisp edges and a tender center, aromatic with ginger, lemongrass and kaffir lime leaves; served with a gently savory ginger-soy dip.
Moc Chau young beef with ginger and lemongrass

Bê chao is a renowned specialty of the Mộc Châu plateau in Son La. Young veal is sliced, seasoned with ginger and lemongrass, then quickly fried in hot oil. Bếp Việt has edited the quantities for a home kitchen and divides the meat into small batches so the outside turns lightly golden while the inside stays tender.

Drain the veal briefly on paper towels and serve immediately with crisp ginger, lemongrass and kaffir lime leaves. Serve the ginger-fermented-soy dip on the side with fresh greens to balance the richness.
One shared platter for four, served hot with rice or fresh greens.
About one hour, including preparation, a 20-minute marinade, quick-frying in batches and mixing the dipping sauce.
fried veal with ginger and lemongrass
Cut the meat into pieces of even thickness and pat them dry before frying for even cooking and less oil splatter.
Fry in small batches in moderately hot oil; do not let the oil smoke. Thicker pieces need enough time for the center to cook through.
Fry the ginger, lemongrass and kaffir lime leaves separately for only a short time and remove them as soon as fragrant to avoid bitterness. Do not pour raw marinade over the cooked dish.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Quảng Nam young jackfruit and flying-fish soup
Young jackfruit soup with flying fish
Quảng Nam jackfruit and fish soup
fields: Pale golden young-jackfruit wedges and intact cooked flying-fish pieces sit in lightly golden broth, finished with scallion and herbs.
Young jackfruit soup with flying fish
Quảng Nam jackfruit and fish soup

This rustic soup pairs young jackfruit from the garden with flying fish from Quảng Nam’s coast. The fruit turns tender and nearly translucent while the fish gives the broth gentle sweetness. Bếp Việt adapts the water and seasoning for a home-sized pot, keeping the broth light.
Ladle broth and solids into bowls and serve hot with steamed rice. Offer green-chili fish sauce separately if desired; season lightly so the jackfruit remains distinct.
One pot for four people, shared with hot rice as part of a family meal.
About 45 minutes to prepare the ingredients and simmer the soup.
If handling fresh jackfruit, lightly oil the knife and hands to reduce sticky sap; soak the cut pieces in lightly salted water and rinse.
Choose fresh flying fish or fish cleaned by the seller; remove gills and entrails and pat dry.
Add fish first and stir gently; add jackfruit once the fish begins to firm so the pieces do not break.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Hue braised pork belly with fermented shrimp paste
Hue pork belly braised with mắm ruốc
Thịt kho mắm ruốc miền Trung
fields: Amber-brown pork cubes are coated in glossy reduced shrimp-paste sauce, fragrant with lemongrass and garlic and lightly accented with chili.
Hue pork belly braised with mắm ruốc
Thịt kho mắm ruốc miền Trung

Pork belly is first browned so some fat renders, then gently braised with lemongrass, garlic and thinned mắm ruốc. Bếp Việt moderates the salt and sweetness so the paste’s distinctive aroma stays clear without becoming harsh.
Serve hot with steamed rice, cucumber or boiled greens. The braise is already savory; use a clean spoon for leftovers.
A savory braise for four, served with rice and vegetables.
About 65 minutes including a brief 10-minute seasoning rest.
pork belly braised with shrimp paste
Mắm ruốc varies in saltiness; dilute and strain if needed, then season with only part of the amount first.
Render pork over medium heat; drain some fat if necessary but keep a little to fry the aromatics.
Braise over low heat until the sauce coats the pork; do not cook it completely dry.

names: Hue duck eggs um with bottle gourd
Hue duck eggs braised with bottle gourd
fields: A hot bowl of fully cooked duck eggs and tender pale-green bottle-gourd pieces in broth scented with ginger and Vietnamese coriander.
Hue duck eggs braised with bottle gourd

Duck eggs are um-cooked with young bottle gourd, Hue fermented shrimp paste, ginger and Vietnamese coriander. Bếp Việt adapts a small home batch and seasons it gently so the gourd’s sweetness balances the rich eggs and mild salty heat.
Ladle eggs, gourd and broth into bowls. Offer lemon-pepper salt separately if desired; serve immediately while hot.
A small pot for four, served hot as a savory soup or light evening dish with rice.
About 40 minutes to boil the eggs, prepare the gourd and finish the um.
Hue duck eggs and bottle gourd
duck eggs braised with bottle gourd
Choose eggs from a traceable source, wash the shells and boil thoroughly before peeling; remove shell fragments.
Dilute the shrimp paste and add it gradually because salt levels vary.
Add Vietnamese coriander, scallion and ginger near the end; cook the gourd until just tender.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Quỳnh Lưu la lằng soup with shrimp
fields: Dark-green chopped la lằng leaves with cooked pink shrimp and softened tomato in a clear broth, pleasantly bitter with a light savory finish.

La lằng leaves have a gentle bitterness and are used in Quỳnh Lưu, Nghệ An, for a simple soup, especially in hot weather. Bếp Việt adapts a home pot with fresh shrimp and tomatoes. Use only leaves identified and sold as food by a trusted supplier; do not gather unidentified wild leaves.
Serve hot with steamed rice; it pairs well with fried fish and pickled vegetables. Cook only enough for the meal.
One pot for four, served hot with steamed rice.
About 27 minutes to prepare the leaves and shrimp and simmer the soup.
Use only la lằng leaves correctly identified and sold for food by a trusted source; do not substitute unidentified wild leaves.
Add the leaves near the end and avoid prolonged boiling.
If using dried shrimp, soak them first and reduce salt or fish sauce.

names: Hue boiled pork with fermented sour shrimp
Hue-style boiled pork with fermented shrimp
Pork and fig wraps with sour shrimp paste
Boiled pork served with Hue sour shrimp paste
fields: Thin slices of boiled pork are arranged beside pink-red fermented shrimp, fig and green-banana slices, pineapple, cucumber, fresh herbs and rice paper.
Hue-style boiled pork with fermented shrimp
Pork and fig wraps with sour shrimp paste
Boiled pork served with Hue sour shrimp paste

Tender boiled pork belly is served with Hue fermented sour shrimp, fig, green banana, pineapple and herbs for rice-paper wraps. Bếp Việt adapts the portions for a family table, balancing rich pork, tangy shrimp, astringent fig and fresh vegetables.
Wrap pork with herbs, fig and pineapple and dip lightly in the sour shrimp. The condiment is already strongly seasoned, so no extra salty sauce is needed.
A shared platter for four, served with vegetables and rice paper for wrapping.
About 50 minutes to prepare accompaniments, boil and rest the pork, and arrange the platter.
Hue boiled pork with tôm chua
thịt ba chỉ luộc tôm chua
Use ready-to-eat fermented shrimp with clear labeling, source and expiry date; refrigerate as directed and serve with a clean spoon.
Add pork to boiling water, then simmer gently until the center is fully cooked; time depends on thickness.
Rest the pork for 5–10 minutes before slicing so the pieces stay neat and juicy.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Mekong-style braised goby with Vietnamese coriander
Peppery braised goby with Vietnamese coriander
fields: Whole goby are tender and coated in a glossy brown braising sauce; rau ram is fragrant, with a warm finish of pepper and chili.
Peppery braised goby with Vietnamese coriander

Braised goby with Vietnamese coriander is a familiar Southern Vietnamese family meal. Small goby are gently simmered with fish sauce, pepper and layers of rau ram so the herb infuses the fish. Bếp Việt standardizes the amounts for four servings and uses coconut caramel for a glossy brown finish in a clay or heavy-bottomed pot.
Serve hot in the clay pot with steamed rice. Add cucumber or boiled vegetables to balance the savory-sweet sauce.
One small clay pot of braised fish for four people, served with steamed rice and boiled vegetables.
About 50 minutes, including preparation, marinating and gentle braising.
Choose fresh fish and ask the fishmonger to clean it; rinse briefly, then drain well before seasoning.
Marinate for about 15 minutes and layer rau ram between the fish; gently shake the pot instead of stirring so the fish stays intact.
Fish sauce saltiness varies. Taste the sauce before reducing it, and add hot water if the pot dries too quickly.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Southern Vietnamese bottle-gourd soup with dried shrimp
Mekong-style gourd and dried shrimp soup
Bottle gourd and dried shrimp soup with scallions
fields: A clear, lightly sweet broth with tender pale-green gourd slices, softened dried shrimp, scallions and cilantro.
Mekong-style gourd and dried shrimp soup
Bottle gourd and dried shrimp soup with scallions

Bottle-gourd soup with dried shrimp is a gently sweet soup often served with Southern Vietnamese home meals. The dried shrimp are soaked and simmered first to build a naturally savory broth; the gourd is added near the end so it stays green and just tender. This Bếp Việt version uses thin slices for easy preparation and everyday cooking.
Ladle the hot soup into a bowl and finish with scallions and cilantro. Serve with steamed rice and a braised or roasted dish.
Four bowls of light soup, served hot with a family meal.
About 40 minutes, including soaking the shrimp and simmering the broth.
Soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes and rinse to remove surface grit and excess salt; strain and reserve the soaking water if you want a stronger broth.
Add the gourd only after the broth is boiling and cook until just tender; overcooking makes it mushy and clouds the soup.
Taste before adding fish sauce because dried shrimp can already be salty.
Rau thơm và phần ăn kèm

names: Pan-roasted freshwater shrimp with lime leaf
Tiny freshwater shrimp stir-fried with lime leaves

Tép đồng rang lá chanh is a rustic dish of tiny freshwater shrimp dry-roasted first, then finished with rendered pork fat, shallot and lime leaf. The Bếp Việt family version uses a restrained sweet-salty seasoning and keeps the two-stage roasting method so the shrimp dry before they are seasoned.
Serve hot as a small side dish with steamed rice, boiled greens or vegetable soup. Add a little lime juice if you prefer a brighter finish.
One small plate of crisp shrimp to serve with steamed rice and boiled vegetables.
About 35 minutes, including cleaning, dry-roasting and seasoning the shrimp.
Choose fresh shrimp, rinse well and drain completely; remaining water makes the shrimp take longer to dry.
Dry-roast over medium-high heat until the shrimp turn pink and dry, then add the fat and seasoning so they remain crisp rather than tough.
Slice the lime leaf very finely and add it at the end to preserve its aroma.

fields: Tender grilled eggplant with a few charred purple edges, topped with scallion oil, garlic-chili fish sauce and a little crushed roasted peanut.
Grilled eggplant with scallion oil and fish sauce

Grilled eggplant with scallion oil is a familiar Southern Vietnamese vegetable side. The eggplant is grilled until tender, its charred skin is peeled back, then it is dressed with scallion oil and garlic-chili fish sauce. This Bếp Việt home version keeps the simple presentation and offers roasted peanuts as an optional finish.
Split the eggplant lengthwise and serve whole or cut into pieces. Eat warm with steamed rice as a vegetable side.
One plate of split grilled eggplant to serve as a vegetable side for four.
About 30 minutes, including preparing the eggplant, grilling and making scallion oil.
Choose firm, glossy eggplant of moderate size so the flesh softens before the skin becomes too charred.
For an oven version, preheat to 220°C and turn the eggplant once; test with a skewer to ensure the flesh is fully tender.
Pour hot oil over the scallions so they soften but stay green; season the fish sauce lightly because the eggplant absorbs it quickly.

Mekong-style kho quet with dried shrimp and pork cracklings

Kho quẹt with dried shrimp and pork cracklings is a savory dipping sauce associated with everyday Southern Vietnamese meals. Dried shrimp, fish sauce and pepper are gently simmered until lightly thickened, then the crisp pork is added for richness. Bếp Việt balances the salty-sweet sauce for a family serving and pairs it with boiled vegetables.
Set the small pot in the middle of the table and dip the boiled vegetables a little at a time. Serve with steamed rice or crisp rice cakes if desired.
One small pot of kho quẹt with a plate of boiled vegetables for four people to share with rice.
About 45 minutes, including soaking the shrimp, rendering pork, simmering the sauce and boiling vegetables.

Render the pork over medium heat until crisp but not burnt; drain most of the fat and keep only about one tablespoon to sauté the aromatics.
Once the fish-sauce mixture begins to thicken, lower the heat and turn it off slightly early because the sauce will continue to thicken as it cools.

This familiar Northern Vietnamese summer soup pairs tender pork ribs and tomatoes with the clean sourness of green dracontomelon. The fruit is simmered separately and mashed so its acidity can be added gradually; scallion and Vietnamese coriander finish the broth.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a savory main dish. Add the dracontomelon liquid gradually so the soup stays pleasantly sour rather than sharp.
One pot of gently sour soup for four people to share with a family meal.

Blanch and rinse the ribs for a clearer broth.
Simmer and mash the dracontomelon separately, then strain and add its liquid a little at a time.
Add scallions and Vietnamese coriander at the end to keep their aroma.

Rice-field perch braised with B?n soybean and starfruit

Rice-field perch braised with B?n soybean and starfruit

This Northern-style braise combines the savory depth of Bần fermented soybean paste with the mild tartness of green starfruit. The fish is layered with starfruit and simmered gently until firm and coated in a lightly thickened sauce; turmeric leaf adds a regional aroma when available.
Serve hot in the clay pot with steamed rice and boiled greens. Taste before adding extra salt because fermented soybean paste varies in saltiness.
Three or four small tilapia braised with starfruit for four servings.
About 90 minutes when cooked sequentially; parallel prep can shorten the total time.
tilapia braised with fermented soybean paste and starfruit
Sweet leaf soup with minced pork
Drain the fish well and avoid turning it while braising so it stays intact.

Chicken steamed with lá trúc is a rustic dish associated with the Bảy Núi area of An Giang. The leaves and fruit have a stronger, more aromatic citrus character than ordinary lime; steaming the seasoned chicken over the leaves keeps the meat moist and fragrant.
Chop the chicken just before serving and eat hot with fresh vegetables or shredded banana blossom. Serve the chili salt separately for dipping.
One 1.2 kg free-range chicken, divided into four servings.

Bright green luffa slices that are tender but not mushy, coated with softly set egg and finished with scallion and pepper.

Stir-fried luffa with egg is a quick home-style side dish: tender, juicy luffa and soft golden egg come together with scallion. Cooking the luffa only until just tender preserves its green color and natural sweetness.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a more savory main. This dish is best just after cooking because the luffa releases liquid as it stands.
One shared vegetable side dish for four people.
About 20 minutes when cooked sequentially; parallel prep can shorten the total time.
Choose young, firm luffa and cut it thick enough to hold its shape.
Keep the pan hot and add the egg when the luffa is nearly tender.
Stop stirring as soon as the egg has set to keep the luffa from becoming watery.

Taro soup with peanuts and tofu
fields: A mild broth with tender taro, nutty peanuts and tofu pieces that hold their shape, finished with fresh Vietnamese coriander.
Vegetarian taro soup with peanuts and tofu
Taro soup with peanuts and tofu

This simple vegetarian soup combines the earthy sweetness of taro and peanuts with golden fried tofu and fragrant Vietnamese coriander. Simmer the peanuts until tender before adding the taro so the ingredients finish cooking together without the taro breaking apart.
Ladle into a large bowl and serve hot with steamed rice and a vegetable or braised vegetarian dish. If starting with dried peanuts, soak and boil them separately first.
One pot of mild vegetarian soup for four people to share.

A Northern Vietnamese fish soup made sour with roasted doc fruit, with tender fish, tomato, dill and scallions. Bếp Việt standardizes the home-size method and adds the strained doc juice gradually so its tartness is easy to adjust.
Lift the fish gently into a deep bowl, ladle over hot broth and serve with steamed rice. Boiled greens are an easy side.
One pot of soup, about four bowls, served with steamed rice.

Roast the doc fruit until soft, remove its charred skin, mash and strain; add the juice a little at a time.

A seasonal Song Da fish dish combining small silver fish with minced pork, egg and herbs, shallow-fried into golden patties. Bếp Việt edits the family-size recipe, keeping the fish's delicate sweetness and the aroma of betel leaf, Vietnamese coriander and dill.
Serve hot with steamed rice, fresh greens and sweet-sour fish sauce or chili sauce.
About 12–16 small patties for four people with rice.

Rinse the small fish gently and drain them well to keep the mixture from becoming watery.
Add cornstarch just until the mixture holds together; add a little at a time if needed.

names: Crispy small goby with wild betel leaf
fields: Golden, crisp small fish that are drained of excess oil, paired with aromatic betel leaf and balanced dipping sauce.

Braised roast pork and sour mustard greens

names: Lai Chau Thai Grilled Stream Moss
fields: Soft, slightly chewy and moist moss scented with lemongrass, ginger, mắc khén and grilled leaves; the leaves are darkened while the filling stays unburnt.

Edible stream moss is rinsed and pounded to remove grit, squeezed dry, seasoned with lemongrass, ginger, chili and highland spices, then wrapped in dong leaves and grilled. Bếp Việt adapts the dish into small parcels that cook evenly at home.
